top_choice_rationale: P003 (Autor, Dorn, Hanson) is, in my judgement, the achievement with the sharpest attribution and the most heavily tested evidence. The jointly authored China-shock papers share one design and one data setup, so the credit trail points to three people. Their central finding is that local adjustment to trade and technology shocks is slow and costly. That contradicted the expectation of fast reallocation and has survived one to three decades of replication and criticism of shift-share inference. The finding is mature and has influenced labour, trade and public economics and the policy debate. With the citation limited to empirical evidence on labour demand and local adjustment, it avoids the task-model theory that sits partly with Acemoglu and Restrepo, and it avoids the skill-premium literature that overlaps with earlier prizes. Katz's omission is a real cost, and the size and persistence of the effects are still debated. P001 (a Kiyotaki-Moore pair) is the cleanest attribution and a foundational mechanism, but direct identification of the collateral channel is mixed and it sits near the 2022 prize. P002 (Berry, Levinsohn, Pakes) has a clean core and a long applied record, but it carries a visible omission of Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin and depends on functional-form assumptions. The margins between all three are narrow and rest on weighting, not on a decisive difference in quality. I rank P000 last because each of the three proposals describes a mature, well-attributed and consequential achievement.
recusal_note: My profile lists no co-authorship or institutional tie to Autor, Dorn, Hanson, Kiyotaki, Moore, Berry, Levinsohn or Pakes. My field of empirical labour economics and policy evaluation is close to P003, and my 2021 presentation speech praised natural-experiment designs, which may predispose me toward this style of evidence. I have tried to apply the same criteria to every proposal. Disclosed, not adjudicated.
